caption: The four Unit Telescopes of the Very Large Telescope under the Milky Way, Paranal Observatory
story: Four large, angular enclosures stand on bare mountain ground while an orange glow from the Sun lifts over the horizon. Above them the Milky Way arcs right across the panorama and bends down until it meets the land. The buildings house the Unit Telescopes of ESO's Very Large Telescope, set in the remote mountains of Chile's Atacama Desert.

Our galaxy holds hundreds of billions of stars, but its band looks patchy rather than smooth. That mottling comes from vast clouds of dust between the stars, which block the light of stars lying farther away. The sky behind the bright points of light also carries a faint red and green airglow.

Each Unit Telescope can observe on its own from Paranal Observatory. The four can also be combined and used together, and working as a team they behave like one telescope whose mirror is effectively up to 130 metres wide.
explore: The site lies far from civilisation in the Atacama Desert. The Sun's glow on the horizon is faint next to the display of stars and galactic light filling the sky overhead.

understand.summary: A ground-based landscape photograph by Y. Beletsky for ESO, taken in visible light. No colour mapping is involved, as the colours are those the camera recorded.
understand.eye: A camera exposure gathers more light than the eye can, so the airglow and the texture of the Milky Way look stronger than they would to someone standing on the site.

scaleExtra: Working together, the four Unit Telescopes act like a single telescope with an effective mirror up to 130 metres across, according to ESO.
alt: Four angular telescope enclosures on a barren mountain ridge beneath the arching band of the Milky Way, with an orange glow on the horizon and faint red and green airglow in the sky.

caption: Twilight and the Milky Way over the Very Large Telescope, Paranal Observatory
story: A band of fiery colour lines the horizon close to Paranal Observatory in northern Chile, and it washes the four Unit Telescopes of ESO's Very Large Telescope in a soft peach light. The Milky Way seems to rise straight up out of one of the telescopes, with stars crowded on both sides. ESO Photo Ambassador Babak Tafreshi took the photograph.

The dazzling star at the top is Sirius, part of Canis Major, the Greater Dog. It is the brightest star in our sky, and it is really a pair. One member is a main-sequence star in the steady middle of its life, burning nuclear fuel. The other is a white dwarf, the dense remains of a star whose fuel ran out long ago.
Lower down, beside the Milky Way, three stars in a row form Orion's belt. Betelgeuse, a red giant, lies to the right of it and the pink glow of the Orion Nebula sits to the left.
explore: Farther down, past the face of Taurus the Bull, a tight knot of stars sits over the glowing horizon. These are the Pleiades, also called the Seven Sisters, an open cluster whose light is dominated by hot, blue B-type stars. It is among the nearest star clusters to Earth. Just beneath it, a small open dome belonging to a VLT Auxiliary Telescope points at the sky.

understand.summary: A ground-based landscape photograph by Babak Tafreshi for ESO, taken in visible light. The colours are those the camera recorded.
understand.eye: A camera exposure collects more light than the eye, so the Milky Way and the pink glow of the Orion Nebula appear brighter here than they would to a visitor on the mountain.

alt: Four telescope enclosures lit by a peach-coloured glow from a fiery band on the horizon, with the Milky Way rising from one of them and a bright star at the top of the frame.

caption: Sprites seen from the Very Large Telescope platform, Paranal Observatory
story: ESO Photo Ambassador Petr Horálek caught sprites from the platform of the Very Large Telescope at Paranal Observatory. Sprites are rare flashes in the upper atmosphere, and they usually appear as clusters of red-orange light.

They form high above thunderstorms, at altitudes of about 80 kilometres, and are linked to irregularities in the ionosphere. What sets them off is positive cloud-to-ground lightning. This kind of strike is less common and more powerful than the negative sort, because its discharge starts near the top of the cloud, farther from the ground.

A sprite lasts only a fraction of a second. In that brief burst it shoots downward and trails red tendrils before vanishing. The one Horálek photographed was most likely more than 500 kilometres away and spanned a height of up to 80 kilometres. The storm behind it was over Argentina, as a satellite image of the storm shows.

understand.summary: A ground-based landscape photograph by Petr Horálek for ESO, taken in visible light. The colours are those the camera recorded.
understand.eye: A sprite lasts only a fraction of a second, so an eye would catch at most a brief flicker, while the camera holds its shape in a single frame.

scaleExtra: The sprite was most likely more than 500 kilometres away and spanned a height of up to 80 kilometres, according to ESO.
alt: Sprites in the night sky, photographed from the Very Large Telescope platform at Paranal Observatory.

caption: A red sprite and the Magellanic Clouds over La Silla Observatory
story: A clear night sky over ESO's La Silla Observatory is tinted with red and green airglow. Just right of centre sit the Small and Large Magellanic Clouds, and rosy-red glows mark several star-forming regions. A faint green streak just left of the Milky Way is a meteor.

The most unusual feature is much closer to home. Low on the left horizon is a sprite, a rare flash in the upper atmosphere. Sprites happen high above storm clouds, at about 80 kilometres up, and are tied to irregularities in the ionosphere. They tend to show up as groups of red-orange flashes.

Positive cloud-to-ground lightning sets them off. That kind is rarer and stronger than the negative kind because the discharge begins in the upper part of the cloud. The sprite darts downward, trails red tendrils and disappears within a fraction of a second.
explore: This sprite was most likely more than 500 kilometres from the camera and spanned a height of up to 80 kilometres. The storm that produced it was over Argentina, as a satellite image of the storm shows. The photograph is by ESO Photo Ambassador Petr Horálek.

understand.summary: A ground-based landscape photograph by Petr Horálek for ESO, taken in visible light. The colours are those the camera recorded.
understand.eye: A camera exposure gathers more light than the eye, so faint features such as the airglow register more strongly, while the fleeting sprite would be only a brief flicker to a watcher.

scaleExtra: The sprite was most likely more than 500 kilometres away and spanned a height of up to 80 kilometres, according to ESO.
alt: A cloudless night sky over La Silla Observatory with red and green airglow, the Milky Way, the two Magellanic Clouds right of centre, a faint green meteor streak and a red sprite on the left horizon.

caption: Sprites over La Silla Observatory
story: Petr Horálek, one of ESO's Photo Ambassadors, photographed these sprites at ESO's La Silla Observatory. Sprites are rare events in the upper atmosphere and usually appear as groups of red-orange flashes high above a storm.

They occur at altitudes of about 80 kilometres and are caused by irregularities in the ionosphere. The trigger is positive cloud-to-ground lightning. Compared with the more familiar negative lightning, it is less frequent and more powerful, because its discharge comes from the top of the cloud rather than the lower part near the ground.

Once triggered, a sprite grows quickly downward, sending out dangling red tendrils, and then it is gone. The whole event lasts only a fraction of a second, which makes sprites hard to catch on camera.
explore: The sprite in this photograph was most likely more than 500 kilometres away and stretched over a height of up to 80 kilometres. The storm behind it was over Argentina, as a satellite image of the storm shows.

understand.summary: A ground-based landscape photograph by Petr Horálek for ESO, taken in visible light. The colours are those the camera recorded.
understand.eye: Because a sprite lasts only a fraction of a second, an observer would see at most a faint flicker, whereas the camera records its shape and colour.

scaleExtra: The sprite was most likely more than 500 kilometres away and spanned a height of up to 80 kilometres, according to ESO.
alt: Sprites in the night sky above La Silla Observatory.

caption: Yepun and an Auxiliary Telescope on the Very Large Telescope platform
story: Two telescopes share this night scene on the platform of ESO's Very Large Telescope. The large one is the fourth Unit Telescope, known as Yepun, and it is sending a laser beam up into the sky. To the right stands a much smaller companion, one of the Auxiliary Telescopes.

The laser creates what astronomers call a guide star. It is part of the telescope's adaptive optics system, which measures how the turbulent air above the site is blurring starlight and corrects for that disturbance. With the blurring removed, the telescope can study the sky in far greater detail than it otherwise could.

The smaller instrument is the second of four Auxiliary Telescopes on the platform, each with a mirror 1.8 metres across. They are modest beside the Unit Telescopes, but they belong to the same observatory and share the same platform.
explore: The photograph is credited to A. Ghizzi Panizza for ESO. Adaptive optics is the general name for systems that adjust a telescope's optics to cancel out atmospheric blurring, and the laser guide star gives the system a reference point to measure against.

understand.summary: A ground-based photograph by A. Ghizzi Panizza for ESO, taken in visible light. The colours are those the camera recorded.
understand.eye: A camera exposure gathers more light than the eye, so the laser beam and the night sky may look brighter in the photograph than they would to someone on the platform.

alt: A large telescope enclosure firing a laser beam into the night sky, with a smaller telescope standing to the right.

caption: A laser guide star beam from Yepun under the Milky Way, Very Large Telescope
story: A laser beam climbs from Yepun, one of the Unit Telescopes of ESO's Very Large Telescope, and seems to reach far out into space, with the Milky Way in the sky behind. The beam comes from the telescope's Laser Guide Star Facility, a key part of its adaptive optics.

The laser does not travel to the stars. It lights up a spot in Earth's own atmosphere and creates an artificial star there. Astronomers use that artificial star as a reference, because its light passes through the same turbulent air as light from the objects they are studying.

Turbulence in the atmosphere blurs starlight and can spoil the quality of the data a telescope collects. By watching how the artificial star is distorted, the adaptive optics system can correct for that turbulence, which lets Yepun record sharper observations than it could without the laser.
explore: The facility on Yepun is officially called the Laser Guide Star Facility. The panorama is credited to A. Ghizzi Panizza for ESO.

understand.summary: A ground-based panoramic photograph by A. Ghizzi Panizza for ESO, taken in visible light. The colours are those the camera recorded.
understand.eye: A camera exposure collects more light than the eye, so the Milky Way appears richer in the photograph than it would to someone standing beside the telescope.

alt: A laser beam shooting up from a large telescope enclosure into a night sky crossed by the Milky Way.

caption: Comet C/2023 A3 (Tsuchinshan-ATLAS) beyond the Extremely Large Telescope, Atacama Desert
story: A helmet-shaped dome rises from Chile's Atacama Desert, and far off on the horizon a bright white streak is shaped like an arrow. The dome belongs to ESO's Extremely Large Telescope, or ELT, and the streak is comet C/2023 A3 (Tsuchinshan-ATLAS).

The ELT's dome was still under construction when this was taken and had not yet been fully clad, though the work of covering it was advancing quickly. The unfinished dome faces no threat from its visitor, which was simply passing on its path around the Sun.

Skywatchers on Earth could see the comet during September and October 2024. After that it set off on a long trip home to the Oort Cloud, on the outskirts of the Solar System. Comets are icy bodies, and their bright tails form when the Sun's heat drives material off them.
explore: The picture comes from one of the webcams that watch over the ELT, and it was captured on 30 September 2024. The comet's full designation is C/2023 A3, with Tsuchinshan-ATLAS as its name.

understand.summary: A frame from one of the ELT webcams, recorded in visible light. The colours are those the camera recorded.
understand.eye: The webcam records visible light, as the eye does, although a camera can pick up a faint comet tail more easily than the eye.

alt: A large, partly clad helmet-shaped dome in the desert with a bright white comet on the horizon.

caption: Evening at Paranal Observatory with the first VLT Unit Telescopes under construction
story: Telescope domes stand on the summit of Paranal in the fading light, about half an hour after sunset. Through the slit of one dome the structure of UT1, the first Unit Telescope of ESO's Very Large Telescope, can be made out. The next dome holds UT2, well along in its assembly, while the third dome already holds the first parts of UT3.

This is a photograph from the observatory's early days. The plan was that once the Sun set behind the Pacific, the domes would open and the four giant telescopes would turn toward the stars. When the photograph was taken, that was still a goal for the future.

UT1 had just achieved its first light, meaning its first observations of the sky. The other telescopes were due to become operational at regular intervals, and within a few years the first observations were planned with some elements of the VLT Interferometer, which links telescopes together.
explore: ESO described the four working telescopes as a dream that would soon come true. The scene is an evening view of the Paranal site while the Very Large Telescope was still being built.

understand.summary: A ground-based photograph from ESO, taken in visible light. The colours are those the camera recorded.
understand.eye: The picture was taken in twilight, so it shows roughly what a visitor would have seen, although a camera can bring out detail in dim light more readily than the eye.

alt: Telescope domes on a mountaintop at dusk, one with its slit open to show a telescope structure inside.

caption: An Auxiliary Telescope and the Moon at sunset, Very Large Telescope
story: One of the Auxiliary Telescopes of ESO's Very Large Telescope sits in the sunset light with the Moon in the sky nearby. The photograph was taken as the telescope was getting ready for a long night of work.

Its shape and position in the frame give the scene a playful look. Intern Stephen Molyneux liked the picture because the telescope resembles Pacman, the video-game character, about to gobble up the Moon. The resemblance depends on the camera's viewpoint. The telescope and the Moon are, of course, nowhere near each other.

Auxiliary Telescopes are smaller companions to the big Unit Telescopes of the Very Large Telescope. They can be moved around the observing platform, and their light can be combined with that of other telescopes to reveal finer detail than one telescope could manage alone. For a telescope like this one, sunset is when the working night begins.
explore: The photograph is credited to Eric Lagadec for ESO.

understand.summary: A ground-based photograph by Eric Lagadec for ESO, taken in visible light at sunset. The colours are those the camera recorded.
understand.eye: Taken at sunset, the scene is close to what someone on site would see, apart from the framing that lines the Moon up with the telescope.

alt: A small telescope at sunset, framed so that it looks about to swallow the Moon.

caption: The Crab Nebula (Messier 1), imaged by the Very Large Telescope
story: This is the Crab Nebula, also catalogued as Messier 1, as recorded by the VIMOS instrument on ESO's Very Large Telescope. The nebula is the wreckage left behind by a star that exploded in the year 1054, and it is a well-known object.

A remnant like this is the expanding debris of a supernova, the violent death of a star, still spreading through space long after the blast. The Crab lies about 6000 light-years away in the constellation of Taurus. At its centre lies a pulsar, the rapidly spinning collapsed core of the star that exploded.

VIMOS photographed it through three filters, known as V, R and I. The first two sit in visible light and the third reaches toward the near-infrared. Combining the three produces a single colour composite of the whole cloud.
explore: The observations were made on 4 March 2002. Each individual exposure lasted 180 seconds, and the image quality was 0.7 arcseconds. The field covers roughly 7 by 7 arcminutes, with north at the top and east to the left.

understand.summary: Taken with the VIMOS instrument on ESO's Very Large Telescope through V and R filters in visible light and an I filter at the edge of the near-infrared. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: Part of the light was collected in the I band, at the edge of what the eye can see, and the telescope's exposures gather far more light than the eye could from such a faint cloud.

alt: The Crab Nebula, a cloud of debris from an exploded star, photographed by a large ground-based telescope.

caption: The Milky Way above the Paranal Residencia, Paranal Observatory
story: The Milky Way, our home galaxy, glows in the sky over the entrance of the building where astronomers live while they work at ESO's Paranal Observatory. Up in the top left, laser light is visible, coming from Yepun, the fourth Unit Telescope of the Very Large Telescope.

Scenes like this are routine at Paranal. The site has excellent observing conditions and enjoys about 300 clear nights a year, so the sky above the astronomers' lodgings is often as clear as the one shown.

The laser beam has a job to do. It creates an artificial guide star, part of the Very Large Telescope's adaptive optics system. That system corrects for the blurring caused by Earth's atmosphere, which constantly shifts and smears starlight, and it allows the telescope to produce very sharp images.
explore: The photograph is credited to G. Hüdepohl of atacamaphoto.com for ESO, and it carries the title No place like home.

understand.summary: A ground-based landscape photograph by G. Hüdepohl for ESO, taken in visible light. The colours are those the camera recorded.
understand.eye: A camera exposure gathers more light than the eye, so the Milky Way looks brighter and more detailed than it would to someone standing at the entrance.

alt: The Milky Way glowing above the entrance of a building at night, with a laser beam visible in the upper left of the sky.

caption: A Unit Telescope of the Very Large Telescope under a clear night sky, Paranal Observatory
story: One of the four Unit Telescopes of ESO's Very Large Telescope stands under a clear night sky at Paranal Observatory, in a photograph by Daniele Gasparri.

Each Unit Telescope has a main mirror 8.2 metres across, which puts them among the largest single-mirror telescopes in the world. A bigger mirror collects more light, and that lets astronomers study fainter and more distant objects.

The four can observe separately or together. When their light is combined they are equivalent to a single-mirror telescope 16 metres across, effectively the largest optical telescope in the world, according to ESO. The work done here feeds a steady flow of research. On average the Very Large Telescope leads to more than one peer-reviewed scientific paper a day, as astronomers use it to tackle some of the biggest questions about the Universe.
explore: The picture is titled Big questions call for big telescopes, and it is credited to ESO and Daniele Gasparri of astroatacama.com.

understand.summary: A ground-based photograph by Daniele Gasparri for ESO, taken in visible light. The colours are those the camera recorded.
understand.eye: A camera exposure gathers more light than the eye, so the night sky probably shows more stars in the photograph than a visitor would see.

alt: A large telescope enclosure beneath a clear night sky.

caption: The GOODS-South field, imaged by the Very Large Telescope
story: This composite image shows the GOODS-South field, a patch of sky studied in an extremely deep survey with ESO's Very Large Telescope. It contains some of the faintest galaxies ever seen.

The survey used two of the telescope's four giant 8.2-metre units, together with a unique filter built specially for the job. It looked for two kinds of light given off by excited hydrogen atoms, called Lyman-alpha and H-alpha. Both are specific wavelengths that energised hydrogen gives off, and astronomers use them as markers of galaxies where stars are forming.

The results allowed astronomers to work out how much had been missed before. Of the galaxies whose light has taken 10 billion years to arrive, they found that 90% had never been detected. The catalogued distance for the field is a redshift of 2.2.
explore: The data come from two instruments on the Very Large Telescope, FORS and HAWK-I. Lyman-alpha was recorded at 390 nanometres and H-alpha at 2.1 micrometres, which places the H-alpha data in infrared light.

understand.summary: Built from Very Large Telescope data taken with FORS1 at 390 nanometres (Lyman-alpha) and HAWK-I at 2.1 micrometres (H-alpha). The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: The H-alpha data were taken in infrared light, which the eye cannot see, and galaxies this faint are far beyond what any eye could detect.

alt: A deep composite image of a field of sky scattered with very faint distant galaxies.

caption: The galaxy cluster MACS J0454.1-0300, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Every bright spot in this Hubble image is a galaxy, and each holds many millions or even billions of stars. Together they form MACS J0454.1-0300, a galaxy cluster. To the left, several objects are stretched into long sweeping arcs.

Galaxy clusters are huge groups of galaxies held together by gravity, and they are among the most massive structures in the Universe. Astronomers put this one's mass at around 180 trillion Suns. So much mass changes the space around it and bends the path of light passing through.

Those arcs are galaxies far behind the cluster. Their light has been amplified on the way to us, but also distorted, and the effect is called gravitational lensing. It makes it possible to see objects so distant that they would otherwise be too faint to detect.
explore: Hubble's Frontier Fields programme was set to use the same effect over the following few years, studying very distant objects behind lensing clusters like this one to learn how stars and galaxies took shape and changed in the early Universe. Nick Rose entered a version of this image in the Hubble's Hidden Treasures image processing competition.

understand.summary: Taken with Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys through filters at 555 nanometres in visible light and 814 nanometres in near-infrared light. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: One of the two filters records near-infrared light, which the eye cannot see, and Hubble picks up galaxies far too faint for any eye.

alt: A field of many bright galaxies making up a cluster, with several stretched, curving arcs of light to the left.

caption: The Milky Way over a snowy La Silla Observatory
story: Winter has come to ESO's La Silla Observatory, and above it the plane of the Milky Way slants across the frame in a spray of stars. Reading from right to left, the domes belong to the ESO 3.6-metre telescope, then the 3.58-metre New Technology Telescope (NTT), then the ESO 1-metre Schmidt telescope, and finally the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope, whose dome carries a layer of snow.

La Silla sits on the edge of the Atacama Desert at an altitude of 2400 metres, far from the lit-up cities of northern Chile. After sunset its skies turn pitch-black, and that darkness makes it one of the best places for astronomy.

Even a site this high, dry and remote gets weather. In the winter months snow can blanket the peak and the telescope domes. The high ESO sites see both hot and cold temperatures over the year and at times face harsh conditions.
explore: Next to the dome of the ESO 3.6-metre telescope is the small dome of the Coudé Auxiliary Telescope, which is no longer in use. Between it and the NTT are the observatory's water tanks. ESO Photo Ambassador José Francisco Salgado took the photograph.

understand.summary: A ground-based landscape photograph by José Francisco Salgado for ESO, taken in visible light. The colours are those the camera recorded.
understand.eye: A camera exposure collects more light than the eye, so the Milky Way appears fuller and brighter than it would to someone standing on the mountain.

alt: Wintry telescope domes on a mountaintop, one carrying snow, with the band of the Milky Way slanting across the starry sky above.

caption: Morning sunlight on Cerro Paranal, home of the Very Large Telescope
story: The first rays of the morning Sun fall on Cerro Paranal in northern Chile, the mountain that is home to ESO's Very Large Telescope. The photograph, by Gerhard Hüdepohl, carries the title A sea of clouds.

Dawn at an observatory marks the end of the working day rather than the start. Sunrise here signals that another successful night of observations has finished, and the telescopes stop collecting light until evening comes round again.

ESO describes the Very Large Telescope as the most productive ground-based astronomical facility in the world. Paranal lies in the Atacama Desert, a high and dry region where clear skies are common, which is why observatories are built there. The telescopes do their work in the dark hours, so sunrise over the mountain is the moment the night shift ends.

understand.summary: A ground-based landscape photograph by Gerhard Hüdepohl for ESO, taken in visible light. The colours are those the camera recorded.
understand.eye: Taken in daylight at sunrise, the scene is probably close to what someone on the mountain would see.

alt: The summit of Cerro Paranal lit by the first rays of the morning Sun.

caption: The Milky Way arching between two telescopes, La Silla Observatory
story: The band of the Milky Way blazes across the sky and forms a bridge between two telescopes at ESO's La Silla Observatory. The ESO 3.6-metre telescope stands on the left and the Swedish-ESO Submillimetre Telescope on the right. In the upper right corner the Large and Small Magellanic Clouds, a pair of nearby galaxies, sit together above the galactic plane.
The bright red splash at the centre of the frame is the Gum Nebula. In the lower left, a particularly bright dot is the planet Jupiter.

ESO Photo Ambassador Petr Horálek took this panorama. He said he had wondered whether the colours of the Universe could be captured without complicated equipment, and he was first inspired by one of the posters for Christopher Nolan's film Interstellar. He added that at La Silla it is possible to feel, and to photograph, interstellar moments.
explore: The picture carries the title Inspired by Interstellar. ESO calls La Silla photogenic from every angle, including creative viewpoints such as this panoramic one.

understand.summary: A ground-based panoramic photograph by Petr Horálek for ESO, taken in visible light. The photographer set out to work without complicated equipment. The colours are those the camera recorded.
understand.eye: A camera exposure gathers more light than the eye, so the red of the Gum Nebula and the brightness of the Milky Way are stronger here than a person would see.

alt: A panoramic view of the Milky Way arching between two telescopes, with a red nebula in the middle of the sky, two small galaxies in the upper right and a bright dot in the lower left.

caption: The ESO 3.6-metre telescope at La Silla Observatory
story: The subject of this photograph by Zdeněk Bardon is the 3.6-metre telescope at ESO's La Silla Observatory in Chile, a telescope that has become a home for planet hunters.

The telescope is home to the High Accuracy Radial velocity Planet Searcher, known as HARPS, which ranks among the world's most successful instruments for finding planets. Instruments of this kind look for tiny, regular shifts in a star's light caused by an orbiting planet tugging the star back and forth.

In mid-2022 a second instrument on the same telescope made its first observations, known as first light. This is the Near InfraRed Planet Searcher, or NIRPS. It works alongside HARPS in the search for planets and focuses on rocky worlds orbiting red dwarf stars. Red dwarfs are small, cool stars, and they give off much of their light in the infrared, which is where NIRPS is designed to look.

understand.summary: A ground-based photograph by Zdeněk Bardon for ESO, taken in visible light. The colours are those the camera recorded.
understand.eye: The camera records visible light, the kind the eye sees, whereas NIRPS studies near-infrared light that the eye cannot detect.

alt: The ESO 3.6-metre telescope at La Silla Observatory.

caption: Comet NEOWISE and noctilucent clouds above ESO Headquarters, Garching
story: A comet hangs in the sky above ESO's Headquarters and the ESO Supernova building in Garching, Germany. It is nicknamed NEOWISE and comes from the outer reaches of the Solar System. It shares the sky with noctilucent clouds, shiny and icy clouds that look much like ripples on water.

The comet's official name is C/2020 F3. It was discovered in March 2020 by NASA's NEOWISE space mission, which gave it its nickname. Its bright tail forms because the Sun's heat is boiling away the outer layers of the icy comet.

NEOWISE had already come through its closest approach to the Sun, on 3 July 2020. There was still a risk that it might break apart as it swung away from the Sun's heat. If it stays in one piece it will head back to the cold outer Solar System, and astronomers do not expect it back for about another 6800 years.
explore: The comet was expected to fade through July but stay visible to the naked eye all month. It was due to make its closest approach to Earth on 23 July, passing at a distance of just over 100 million kilometres.

understand.summary: A ground-based photograph by S. Ströbele for ESO, taken in visible light. The colours are those the camera recorded.
understand.eye: The comet was visible to the naked eye, but a camera exposure gathers more light and shows the tail and the noctilucent clouds more clearly than an eye would.

scaleExtra: The comet's closest approach to Earth was expected to be just over 100 million kilometres, according to ESO.
alt: A comet with a bright tail in the night sky above modern buildings, with rippled, shining clouds nearby.

caption: Comet NEOWISE over the ESO Supernova and ESO Headquarters, Garching
story: Comet NEOWISE shines above ESO's Headquarters and the neighbouring ESO Supernova in Garching, Germany, in a photograph by R. Shida. Alongside it are noctilucent clouds, a very unusual sight at night. These icy clouds shine and have a rippled look, rather like the surface of water.

NEOWISE travelled in from the far reaches of the Solar System. Its formal designation is C/2020 F3, and it was first found in March 2020 by NASA's NEOWISE space mission, which lent the comet its nickname. The glowing tail comes from the Sun's heat, which evaporates the outer layers of the icy nucleus.

By the time of this photograph the comet had already survived its closest pass by the Sun, on 3 July 2020. It could still have broken up as it sped away from the heat. If it holds together it will return to the icy outer Solar System and is not expected back for approximately another 6800 years.
explore: At the time, the comet was expected to grow fainter as July went on while remaining a naked-eye object for the whole month. Its closest point to Earth was due on 23 July, at just over 100 million kilometres.

understand.summary: A ground-based photograph by R. Shida for ESO, taken in visible light. The colours are those the camera recorded.
understand.eye: NEOWISE could be seen with the naked eye, though a camera exposure collects more light and brings out the tail and the shining clouds more strongly than an eye would.

scaleExtra: The comet's closest approach to Earth was expected to be just over 100 million kilometres, according to ESO.
alt: A comet with a glowing tail above buildings at night, accompanied by shining, rippled clouds.

caption: Auxiliary Telescopes and the Magellanic Clouds, Very Large Telescope
story: Three telescopes with their domes open work in the foreground of this night scene. They are three of the four movable Auxiliary Telescopes at ESO's Very Large Telescope, each with a mirror 1.8 metres across. In the centre of the sky two bright patches mark the Large and Small Magellanic Clouds.
The Magellanic Clouds are neighbouring galaxies to our own, and they are visible to the naked eye. Although they look like soft patches of light, each is a separate galaxy made up of its own stars.

The Very Large Telescope is based on Cerro Paranal in the Atacama Desert of northern Chile. The Auxiliary Telescopes are smaller than the main Unit Telescopes, but because they can be moved they can be placed in different positions on the platform. With domes wide open, as they are in the photograph, they are observing the sky above.
explore: The photograph is credited to M. Claro for ESO and carries the title Domes wide open.

understand.summary: A ground-based landscape photograph by M. Claro for ESO, taken in visible light. The colours are those the camera recorded.
understand.eye: The Magellanic Clouds are visible to the naked eye, but a camera exposure makes them look brighter and more detailed than they would to someone on the platform.

alt: Three small telescopes with open domes in the foreground under a night sky, with two bright patches in the centre.

caption: Twilight colours over the Auxiliary Telescopes, Paranal
story: Colour fills a partly cloudy sky after sunset, and in the foreground stand some of the Auxiliary Telescopes of ESO's Very Large Telescope. The clouds catch the last of the light, which is what produces the show of colour above the observatory.

The Very Large Telescope sits on Cerro Paranal in the Atacama Desert of northern Chile. ESO calls it the world's most advanced optical instrument. It is made up of four Unit Telescopes, each with a main mirror 8.2 metres in diameter, together with four smaller Auxiliary Telescopes like the ones in this photograph.

Twilight is a changeover time at an observatory. The sky is still too bright for most astronomical work, and the telescopes wait for full darkness before they begin the night's observations. M. Claro photographed the Auxiliary Telescopes during that pause between sunset and the start of the observing night.
explore: The picture is titled A twilit display and is credited to M. Claro for ESO.

understand.summary: A ground-based landscape photograph by M. Claro for ESO, taken in visible light. The colours are those the camera recorded.
understand.eye: The twilight colours are real and visible to the eye, although a camera can render them more intensely than a person on site would perceive them.

alt: Small telescopes in the foreground beneath a partly cloudy twilight sky full of colour.

caption: Star trails over Yepun, Very Large Telescope
story: Stars have become trails in this cropped fish-eye photograph of ESO's Very Large Telescope. To the left of Yepun, one of four Unit Telescopes with 8.2-metre mirrors, the Large and Small Magellanic Clouds can just be made out among the trails. Centre right, the Zodiacal Light glows above the horizon.
Star trails appear when a camera records the sky over a long period. As Earth turns, each star moves steadily across the sky and draws an arc in the picture.

The Zodiacal Light is a faint glow produced by sunlight scattering off dust in the Solar System. Here it rises above the Milky Way, which lies below the horizon at the moment the picture was made. A fish-eye lens takes in a very wide field of view, which lets a single frame hold the telescope, the Magellanic Clouds and the Zodiacal Light together. The Very Large Telescope stands on Cerro Paranal in northern Chile's Atacama Desert.
explore: The photograph is credited to M. Claro for ESO.

understand.summary: A ground-based fish-eye photograph by M. Claro for ESO, taken in visible light and cropped. The colours are those the camera recorded.
understand.eye: The eye sees stars as fixed points, while the camera's long exposure turns their slow movement across the sky into trails.

alt: A wide, curved view of a large telescope enclosure under a sky of star trails, with a glow rising right of centre.

caption: The Residencia under the Milky Way, Paranal Observatory
story: A modern building stands in the desert beneath the Milky Way. This is the Residencia, the residence at ESO's Paranal Observatory in Chile, which gives the many professionals and technicians working there a home away from home. The photograph pairs the astronomers' home on Earth with our home galaxy.

German architects Auer+Weber designed the Residencia to fit into the dry Atacama landscape and to interfere as little as possible with astronomical observations. Its sandy colour and modern lines suit the Mars-like terrain around the observatory.

The building has also had a film career. The James Bond film Quantum of Solace chose it as the villain's hideout, and in one of the key scenes the building was destroyed, though only virtually. In reality the building is still standing and is still a home for the people who keep the observatory running.
explore: Paranal Observatory hosts ESO's Very Large Telescope along with four Auxiliary Telescopes. Working together, these telescopes form the Very Large Telescope Interferometer.

understand.summary: A ground-based landscape photograph by Y. Beletsky for ESO, taken in visible light. The colours are those the camera recorded.
understand.eye: A camera exposure gathers more light than the eye, so the Milky Way looks brighter and more textured than it would to a resident stepping outside.

alt: A modern building in an arid desert landscape beneath the band of the Milky Way.

caption: The New Technology Telescope turning during a 30-second exposure, La Silla Observatory
story: The angular enclosure of the New Technology Telescope (NTT) at ESO's La Silla Observatory in Chile is smeared by motion, because the telescope was turning toward its target during a 30-second exposure. Its outside is made of sharp angles rather than the rounded dome most observatories use.

That shape was groundbreaking when the NTT opened in 1989, and its features have since been widely copied, including by ESO's Very Large Telescope. The design aims for the best possible image quality. Carefully controlled ventilation moves air across the telescope and reduces the blurring caused by turbulence inside the building. The large flaps that are part of this system can just be made out in the blur.

The mirror, 3.58 metres across, was never thought of as especially big, but its design was highly innovative. It is flexible and is adjusted continuously to keep a perfect shape, so it cannot sag or flex enough to harm the image. ESO and the NTT pioneered this approach, called active optics, and it is now standard on modern telescopes.
explore: The NTT carries two instruments. SOFI, short for Son of ISAAC after a VLT instrument, is a spectrograph and imaging camera that works in infrared light, and EFOSC2 is a spectrograph and camera built to detect faint objects. La Silla sits 2400 metres up in the southern Atacama Desert, some 600 kilometres to the north of Santiago de Chile. The photograph is by Malte Tewes, an astronomer at Lausanne's Ecole Polytechnique Fédérale in Switzerland, and he shared it through the Your ESO Pictures Flickr group.

understand.summary: A ground-based photograph by Malte Tewes, taken in visible light with a 30-second exposure. The colours are those the camera recorded.
understand.eye: The eye would see the building turn smoothly, while the camera's 30-second exposure records the whole movement at once as a blur.

alt: An angular telescope building blurred by its own rotation, with large flaps just visible in the blur.

caption: An Auxiliary Telescope, the Moon and Venus lined up, Paranal Observatory
story: Three very different spheres line up at ESO's Very Large Telescope at Paranal Observatory in Chile. The largest, in the foreground, is one of the telescope's four Auxiliary Telescopes. Above it floats the Moon, and near the top of the frame is Venus.

The setting Sun lights only a thin sliver of the Moon. Even so, some of the lunar maria can be seen. These are the dark, sea-like areas left by lava flows early in the Moon's history. Venus is the second planet from the Sun and one of Earth's planetary neighbours.

The Auxiliary Telescopes are movable, and they can be arranged in different configurations to suit different scientific goals. From where the photographer stood, this one lined up with the Moon and Venus above it. Astrophotographer and ESO Photo Ambassador Yuri Beletsky caught the alignment during one of his visits to the observatory.
explore: The photograph is titled Spheres on Spheres. Beletsky was fortunate to catch the three objects lined up in the sky.

understand.summary: A ground-based photograph by Yuri Beletsky for ESO, taken in visible light. The colours are those the camera recorded.
understand.eye: The Moon and Venus are both visible to the unaided eye, and it is the camera's viewpoint that lines them up with the telescope.

alt: A spherical telescope enclosure in the foreground with a thin sliver of Moon floating above it and Venus near the top of the sky.

caption: The spiral galaxies NGC 799 and NGC 800, imaged by the Very Large Telescope
story: Two spiral galaxies face us, one above the other. NGC 800 is the upper one and NGC 799 the lower. Both have long arms winding in toward a bright central bulge. Tiny blue dots along the arms are clusters of hot, young stars, while the bulges hold cooler, redder, older stars packed into compact, nearly round regions.

The pair lies about 300 million light-years away in the constellation of Cetus, the Whale. Despite the resemblance they differ in more than size. Only NGC 799 has a bar running out from its bulge, and its two broad, dim arms start at the ends of the bar and wrap almost all the way round, forming a near ring. The smaller NGC 800 has three bright, knotty arms.

Bars are thought to channel gas from the arms to the centre and boost star formation. Galaxies this close typically disturb each other over hundreds of millions of years, and they may eventually merge.
explore: American astronomer Lewis Swift first observed the pair in 1885. A supernova, named SN2004dt, was seen in NGC 799 in 2004. The image comes from the FORS1 instrument on the 8.2-metre Very Large Telescope at Cerro Paranal and combines B, V and R exposures. Five asteroids moved between exposures and left colourful streaks.

understand.summary: Taken with the FORS1 instrument on ESO's Very Large Telescope through B, V and R filters, all in visible light. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: The galaxies are far too faint for the eye, and the telescope's exposures gather light over time to reveal them, which is also why moving asteroids appear as streaks.

alt: Two face-on spiral galaxies, the upper one with three knotty arms and the lower one larger with a central bar and broad arms forming a near ring, with blue dots along the arms and a few colourful streaks.

caption: The Control Building under the rising Milky Way, Paranal Observatory
story: The Control Building at ESO's Paranal Observatory sits in front of the rising Milky Way in this photograph by Y. Beletsky. The building sits on a ledge, or shelf, just beneath the main observing platform on the summit of Paranal.

This building is the real hub of the observatory. Observing teams work here to run the telescopes of the Very Large Telescope and their instruments. From the control room they operate all four Unit Telescopes, the Auxiliary Telescopes and the instruments attached to them.

Doing that takes a great deal of computing. The telescopes and instruments are run through a gigantic series of computers, and these machines fill a whole room beneath the control room. So while the telescopes work on the platform above, the building that runs them sits a little lower down on its shelf of the mountain, with the Milky Way rising behind it.

understand.summary: A ground-based landscape photograph by Y. Beletsky for ESO, taken in visible light. The colours are those the camera recorded.
understand.eye: A camera exposure gathers more light than the eye, so the Milky Way looks brighter behind the building than it would to someone standing outside.

alt: A building on a mountain shelf at night with the Milky Way rising behind it.

caption: The Milky Way over an Auxiliary Telescope, Paranal Observatory
story: The Milky Way stretches across the sky over one of the Auxiliary Telescopes at ESO's Paranal Observatory, in a photograph by Y. Beletsky.
The Auxiliary Telescopes are part of a larger system. Linked with the Very Large Telescope's four Unit Telescopes, they make up the Very Large Telescope Interferometer, or VLTI.

An interferometer brings together the light collected by separate telescopes. Combining them in this way lets astronomers see finer detail than any one of the telescopes could manage alone, because the combined instrument behaves in some ways like a single telescope as wide as the distance between its parts. The Auxiliary Telescopes are much smaller than the Unit Telescopes, but they can be moved around the platform to change that spacing.

understand.summary: A ground-based landscape photograph by Y. Beletsky for ESO, taken in visible light. The colours are those the camera recorded.
understand.eye: A camera exposure gathers more light than the eye, so the Milky Way looks brighter than a visitor would see it.

alt: A small telescope under the band of the Milky Way stretching across the night sky.

caption: A laser guide star beam under the southern Milky Way, Paranal
story: A laser beam rises from the Very Large Telescope into the sky over Paranal, while the southern Milky Way crosses overhead. The constellation of Carina is among those along its path. The photograph is by Petr Horálek.
The beam works as an artificial star. Astronomers use it to correct for disturbance in the atmosphere, the shifting of the air that makes stars twinkle and blurs the images a telescope records.

The idea is that the telescope watches the artificial star, measures how the atmosphere distorts it, and then adjusts to cancel out that distortion for the real objects under study. Because the laser can be pointed where the astronomers need it, the correction does not depend on a bright natural star happening to lie nearby. The result is sharper observations from a telescope on the ground.

understand.summary: A ground-based landscape photograph by Petr Horálek for ESO, taken in visible light. The colours are those the camera recorded.
understand.eye: A camera exposure gathers more light than the eye, so the Milky Way and the laser beam look brighter here than to someone standing on the mountain.

alt: A laser beam shooting up from a telescope into a night sky crossed by the Milky Way.

caption: The hourglass-shaped remnant CK Vulpeculae, imaged by ALMA
story: This image from the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) gives the best view to date of the central part of CK Vulpeculae, an hourglass-shaped remnant. It traces dust and emission in and around the object and reveals its intricate structure. At its heart is a warped, dusty disc, along with gaseous jets that suggest a central system is pushing material outward.

CK Vulpeculae may be the oldest object of its kind ever catalogued. It was first thought to be a nova, but pinning down what it is has proved hard, and several explanations have been tried and dropped. The current view is that it formed when two stars collided, though astronomers still debate what kind of stars they were.

Most novae are explained by runaway explosions between two close stars in a binary system, and CK Vulpeculae never fitted that picture well. These ALMA observations are the first to bring the system into focus and may help settle a 348-year-old mystery.
explore: French monk and astronomer Père Dom Anthelme first spotted the outburst on 20 June 1670, when it was easy to see with the naked eye. Over the next two years it brightened and faded, disappeared and reappeared twice, and then vanished for good. The object lies about 2000 light-years away in the constellation of Vulpecula.

understand.summary: Made with ALMA in its Band 6, which observes millimetre-wavelength light. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: Millimetre-wavelength light is invisible to the eye, so the colours are a translation of signals from dust and gas that no one could see directly.

alt: An hourglass-shaped structure mapped in millimetre-wavelength light, with a warped, dusty disc at its centre.

caption: The ALMA array under a soft-hued sky, Chajnantor Plateau
story: This photograph by D. Kordan shows the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array, known as ALMA, under a sky that the picture's title calls soft-hued.

For studying the cold Universe, ALMA ranks among the most powerful telescopes in the world. Rather than a single mirror it is an array of antennas, which work together to detect millimetre and submillimetre light. That kind of light comes from cold material such as gas and dust, which gives off little visible light.

The array stands on the Chajnantor Plateau in the Atacama Desert in Chile. Water vapour in the air absorbs the kind of light ALMA studies, so a dry, high site suits it well. The photograph pairs the telescope with the colours of the sky above its desert home.

understand.summary: A ground-based landscape photograph by D. Kordan for ESO, taken in visible light. The colours are those the camera recorded.
understand.eye: The camera records visible light much as the eye does, while ALMA itself observes millimetre and submillimetre light that no eye can see.

alt: ALMA antennas on a desert plateau beneath a softly coloured sky.

caption: Unit Telescopes and an Auxiliary Telescope under the Milky Way, Very Large Telescope
story: The Milky Way stretches across the night sky above three of the eight telescopes that make up ESO's Very Large Telescope at Paranal Observatory. Two of the four Unit Telescopes, each with a mirror 8.2 metres across, stand at the back. In front is one of the four Auxiliary Telescopes, whose mirrors are 1.8 metres across.

Each of these telescopes can work on its own. They can also be linked together as the Very Large Telescope Interferometer, or VLTI. An interferometer combines the light gathered by separate telescopes so that together they can pick out finer detail than any of them could alone.

The Auxiliary Telescopes add flexibility to that arrangement. They can be moved across the platform automatically, which means the spacing between the telescopes can be changed from one observation to the next. The photograph, by Y. Beletsky, sets the large and small instruments side by side beneath the band of our own galaxy.

understand.summary: A ground-based landscape photograph by Y. Beletsky for ESO, taken in visible light. The colours are those the camera recorded.
understand.eye: A camera exposure gathers more light than the eye, so the Milky Way looks brighter and more detailed than it would to someone on the platform.

alt: Two large telescope enclosures at the back and a smaller telescope in front, beneath the Milky Way stretching across the night sky.

caption: The MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope under the Milky Way, La Silla Observatory
story: The MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope stands in the foreground at ESO's La Silla Observatory in Chile, with a very bright Milky Way above it. The photograph is by H. Stockebrand.

The telescope has a mixed history. It was first built in Heidelberg, Germany, by the Max Planck Institute for Astronomy. ESO installed it at La Silla and also looks after its upkeep. Since 2003, though, ESO no longer offers observing time on it to its own users, and the Max Planck Society continues to use it.

La Silla was ESO's first venture into Chile, a country whose astronomical conditions ESO describes as perfect. Built in Germany, installed and maintained by ESO, and still used by the Max Planck Society, the 2.2-metre telescope links the two organisations at the site where ESO's work in Chile began.

understand.summary: A ground-based landscape photograph by H. Stockebrand for ESO, taken in visible light. The colours are those the camera recorded.
understand.eye: A camera exposure gathers more light than the eye, so the Milky Way appears brighter than it would to someone standing beside the telescope.

alt: A telescope dome in the foreground beneath a bright band of the Milky Way.

caption: A green-lit ALMA antenna under the Milky Way, Chajnantor Plateau
story: An artificial green glow lights up one of the antennas of the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) as it observes, with the Milky Way above. ALMA has 66 antennas in all, and the photograph, by Babak Tafreshi, is titled Feeling green.

The array stands on the Chajnantor plateau in the Chilean desert, more than 5000 metres above sea level. At that height the air is dry and the atmosphere is thin, and those conditions give an excellent view into the Universe. They make the plateau an ideal home for a telescope as sensitive as this one.

Each antenna is a dish that collects millimetre and submillimetre light, and the signals from many antennas are combined so that they act together as one telescope. The green light on the dish is artificial. It is not produced by the antenna's observations, which record light that no eye can see.

understand.summary: A ground-based landscape photograph by Babak Tafreshi for ESO, taken in visible light. The colours are those the camera recorded, including an artificial green light on the antenna.
understand.eye: The camera records visible light, while the antenna itself observes millimetre and submillimetre light that the eye cannot see.

alt: A large dish antenna lit in green under the Milky Way at night.

caption: The blue compact dwarf galaxy ESO 338-4, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Young blue stars sit inside a cloud of dust and gas at the centre of this Hubble image of ESO 338-4. It is a lonely dwarf galaxy about 100 million light-years away in the constellation of Sagittarius, the Archer, and it belongs to a class called blue compact dwarf galaxies.

Galaxies of this type are named for the intensely blue star-forming regions often found in their cores. One such region lies within ESO 338-4, full of bright young stars that are burning through hydrogen at a furious rate. They are massive, and despite their huge fuel supplies the reactions in their cores will use it up in only millions of years, a very short time by astronomical standards.

The young stars are the product of a recent merger between ESO 338-4 and a wandering galaxy. That encounter stirred up the surrounding clouds of gas and dust and set off a rapid burst of new star formation.
explore: The image is credited to Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3, and the observations also used the Advanced Camera for Surveys and the Space Telescope Imaging Spectrograph. Filters span ultraviolet light at 127 and 152 nanometres, visible light near 500 and 550 nanometres, and near-infrared light at 1.1 micrometres.

understand.summary: Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3, Advanced Camera for Surveys and Space Telescope Imaging Spectrograph observed the galaxy in ultraviolet, visible and near-infrared light. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: Parts of the data were taken in ultraviolet and infrared light, which the eye cannot see, and the galaxy is far too faint to see without a telescope.

alt: A small galaxy with young blue stars in a cloud of dust and gas at its centre.
flags: source caption names the galaxy once as ESO 388-4, likely a typo for ESO 338-4
